title: Impact of exposure to natural versus urban soundscapes on brain functional connectivity, BOLD entropy and behavior
research_question: To investigate the influence of exposure to natural versus urban soundscapes on brain activity (BOLD entropy and whole brain functional connectivity) and behavior (affect and cognitive performance) at rest.

participants.description: 12 female, mean age = 27.6 years, normal or corrected-to-normal vision, not taking psychotropic medication. Participants were from Berlin, Germany.
participants.recruitment: Participant pool of the Max Planck Institute for Human Development

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Forty natural soundscapes (birdsongs, moving water, insects, wind) and forty urban soundscapes (traffic sounds, café ambiance, machinery sounds). Each soundscape was 20s duration with a 500-ms linear fade in and fade out. Amplitude was normalized. Soundscapes were previously categorized as natural/urban.

measures.instrument: z-score average of DNB and DBS performance (post-pre difference)
Pearson's correlation coefficients between ROI time series (Gordon atlas 333 nodes)

findings.antecedent: Listening to urban soundscapes (compared to nature soundscapes)
findings.consequent: Brain Entropy (BEN) in posterior cingulate gyrus, cuneus, precuneus, occipital lobe/calcarine
findings.mechanism: listening to urban sounds increases the complexity of the BOLD signal dynamics.
findings.quote: We found higher BEN when listening to urban sounds in posterior cingulate gyrus, cuneus and precuneus, occipital lobe/calcarine as compared to nature sounds

findings.antecedent: Mean BEN when listening to urban soundscapes
findings.consequent: Change in positive affect (PANAS) from before to after urban sound exposure
findings.mechanism: the higher the BEN, the stronger the decrease in positive affect in the urban sound condition.
findings.quote: We found a negative correlation (p value = 0.04 uncorrected) between the mean entropy when listening to urban sounds and the change in positive affect (PANAS)

findings.antecedent: Listening to nature soundscapes (compared to urban soundscapes)
findings.consequent: Functional Connectivity (FC) between areas in auditory, cinguloopercular, somatomotor hand and mouth networks (Gordon atlas)
findings.mechanism: lower FC between areas in the auditory, cinguloopercular, and somatomotor hand and mouth networks when listening to urban sounds compared to nature sounds
findings.quote: We observed differences in FC, namely, lower FC between areas in the auditory, cinguloopercular, and somatomotor hand and mouth networks when listening to urban sounds compared to nature sounds

findings.antecedent: Mean FC when listening to nature soundscapes (in auditory, cinguloopercular, somatomotor hand and mouth networks)
findings.consequent: Change in composite score of Digit span and N-back (post-pre)
findings.mechanism: a gain in working memory performance is associated with higher connectivity within - among others - the auditory functional brain network while listening to nature.
findings.quote: We observed a positive correlation between the mean FC when listening to nature sounds and difference (post-pre) of the composite score of Digit span and Nback

findings.consequent: Whole brain FC (using anatomical atlas AAL)
findings.quote: No robust differences were found using the anatomical atlas (AAL).

findings.antecedent: Mean BEN when listening to urban sounds
findings.consequent: Change in negative affect (PANAS), cognitive performance (DNB, DBS, composite), or Perceived Stress Scale (PSS)
findings.quote: No correlations were found with the remaining variables (p-values >0.3).

findings.antecedent: Mean FC when listening to nature/urban sounds
findings.consequent: Change in positive/negative affect (PANAS) or Perceived Stress Scale (PSS)
findings.quote: No correlations were found with the remaining variables (p-values >0.15).

mechanisms: Urban sounds convey a lot of uncertainty which might be translated into a more chaotic processing of information, leading to greater Brain Entropy (BEN).
Increased BEN can be an essential driver of neural and cognitive decline.
The brain needs to maintain relatively low levels of BEN to function properly, requiring escape from high entropy states while remaining flexible.
Natural environments are perceived as more coherent and restorative, potentially aligning with enhanced neural information processing.

Higher functional connectivity in auditory, cinguloopercular, somatomotor networks during nature sound exposure is associated with improved working memory performance, suggesting boosted brain processing efficiency.
moderators: Frame-wise displacement (FD) as a covariate for motion
implementation_implications: Exposure to natural soundscapes is associated with gains in cognitive performance and higher functional connectivity.
Exposure to urban soundscapes is associated with increased brain entropy and reduced positive affect, suggesting negative consequences of noise pollution.
limitations: The study lacks the methodological framework to determine whether experience with nature is beneficial or if urbanicity is detrimental, as resting-state brain data was only acquired during soundscape exposure, not before and after.
Future studies should acquire resting-state data before and after natural versus urban soundscape exposure to complement this.
Correlations with behavioral variables did not survive multiple comparison correction and need to be treated with caution.
Further research is needed to unravel the specific active ingredients of auditory stimuli that drive changes in BEN and brain connectivity.
It remains to be investigated whether the effect of soundscapes is due to the sound pattern itself or belief-based construction by the listener.
